titulo: An economic model for the content market in algorithmic social networks
resumo: Why two similar pieces of content yield very different results depending on when they go live, and what that changes in campaign planning.

paragrafos: For organizations that want to position themselves better on social media, take opportunities when they appear and plan campaigns with influencers.
Deciding fast is worth more than producing fast. The time between spotting the opportunity and publishing is made of decision and production, and decision is the part you can shorten.
When the campaign pays per contracted piece, the best moment to publish is before the peak of public attention, not during it.
Competition for attention does not come only from what was published today: old content keeps circulating and taking up space.

titulo: Guide: how to disclose support and advertising in content
resumo: What to say, where to place it and when a support notice is mandatory, with the most common mistakes in videos, stories and text.

paragrafos: Any piece made in exchange for payment, barter, a received product or a paid trip has to say so to the audience. The rule applies to public interest campaigns the same way it applies to consumer products: support from a foundation or an institute is support, and it gets disclosed.
It does not matter whether the supporter asked for the notice or whether the creator agrees with the cause. The criterion is where the money came from, not the opinion of the person publishing.

Content made on the creator's own initiative about a topic already covered in a paid campaign does not need a notice, as long as there is no payment and no request from the supporter. When in doubt, the notice costs less than the suspicion.

Use wording anyone understands on first read: 'advertising', 'paid content', 'supported by' followed by the organization's name. Acronyms, hashtags buried at the end of the caption and terms like 'partnership' or 'collab' do not do the job.

The notice goes at the start, not the end. In video, it appears on screen and is said out loud in the first seconds. In stories, it goes on every card in the sequence, because people may start watching from the middle. In text, it comes before the first paragraph.
When the platform has its own paid content marker, the marker adds to the written notice and does not replace it. The marker disappears in reposts and screenshots; the text stays.

secoes.titulo: Common mistakes and how to fix them
paragrafos: Disclosing only in the first video of a series. Each piece is watched on its own and each piece carries the notice.
Naming the supporter vaguely, as 'a partner organization'. The full name lets the audience look up who paid and weigh the interest behind the message.

Treating the notice as an embarrassment. In the network's tracking, a clear notice did not reduce the reach of the pieces, and it is the criterion supporters use most when deciding to hire the same creator again.

resumo: A verification routine for numbers, quotes and images, sized for the time a creator has between recording and publishing.

secoes.titulo: What to check and in what order
paragrafos: Start with what holds the piece up: the number, the sentence attributed to someone or the central image. If that part falls, the rest is unusable, so it comes first.

Numbers: find the primary source, meaning the table, report or database the number came from, not the article that quoted it. Check unit, period and geographic scope. Most errors the lab reviews are not invented numbers but correct numbers in the wrong context.
Quotes: locate the original record, whether video, audio, document or post. A sentence that exists only in screenshots and reposts is treated as unverified.

Images and video: reverse search in at least two tools, date and location checked against visible elements, and a check for signs of synthetic generation. Material without a confirmed origin goes in as a declared illustration or does not go in.

secoes.titulo: How much time to set aside
paragrafos: A piece with one central figure and one image takes twenty to forty minutes to check for someone who already knows where to look. Book that time in the schedule before recording, not after: finding the error with the video done means recording again.
If there is no time to check everything, cut what was not checked. A piece with two confirmed figures is worth more than one with five figures and one wrong.

For each figure used, keep the link to the primary source, the access date and a screenshot. The record lets you answer a challenge in minutes and is what the supporting organization will ask for if the piece is questioned.
When the source is a person, note name, role and how contact was made. When it is a document, note page and passage.
An error found after publishing is corrected in the same piece, with the correction date visible, not in a new piece that leaves the wrong one online.

titulo: Briefing for organizations: hiring creators without interfering in editing
resumo: What to write in the brief, what to leave out and how to approve a script without turning the creator into a spokesperson.

paragrafos: The brief says what the organization needs the audience to know or do, and for whom. One core message, two at most, each written in a single sentence. If the organization cannot sum it up that way, the problem is the objective, not the creator.

Say what cannot be said: figures the organization does not stand behind, promises it cannot keep, comparisons that create legal risk. That list is the real boundary of the campaign and saves review rounds.
Include the facts and sources the creator may use, with links. The creator should not have to research what the organization already knows.
Delivery deadline, format, number of pieces and fee per piece belong in the contract, not the brief. Mixing the two makes the creator read the brief as a work order.
A finished script, text to read, a shot order. The creator was hired because the audience trusts the way they speak. If the organization writes the lines, it buys the reach and loses the trust.
Adjectives about the organization. The audience does not need to know that the foundation is 'a reference' or 'a pioneer'; it needs to understand the subject.
Exclusivity beyond the campaign period and silence clauses on related topics. Both drive away the most respected creators and do not change the result of the piece.

Approval checks three things: the core message is there, nothing from the list of prohibitions was said and the support is disclosed. Beyond that it is opinion, and opinion is not grounds for rejection.
One review round on the script and one on the final video. Each round has a response deadline for the organization, usually two business days. A missed deadline counts as approval.

Comments go in a list, with the passage quoted and the reason tied to one of the three criteria. 'I did not like the tone' is not a comment; 'the figure at minute two contradicts the source we sent' is.

titulo: Report: how to measure public interest campaigns
resumo: Which indicators show whether a campaign changed what people know or do, and why reach and likes do not answer that question.

secoes.titulo: What reach measures and what it does not
paragrafos: Reach counts how many screens displayed the piece. It does not say whether anyone watched to the end, understood it or did anything different afterwards. For a campaign selling a product that may be enough; for one trying to change a habit or warn about a risk, it is not.

Likes and comments measure reaction to the piece, not to the topic. The report compares twelve public interest campaigns the observatory tracked in 2025 and 2026: the correlation between engagement and change measured in a follow-up survey was weak in ten of them.

Retention and watch time are the platform indicators closest to comprehension. A three-minute piece watched to the end by 40% of the audience informed more than a thirty-second one with three times the reach.

Define before the campaign what needs to change: a fact the audience did not have, an action it was not taking. The indicator comes out of that definition. Without it, any number will do and none will decide.

Measure the baseline before the first piece goes live, with a short survey of the creator's own audience: three questions in a poll or form. Repeat the same survey two weeks after the last piece. The difference is the campaign's result.

When the campaign asks for an action that leaves a trace, such as signing up, consulting a service or using a link, measure the action with a separate link per creator. Cost per action is the indicator that helps most in deciding the next campaign.

Use a comparison group whenever possible: a city, an age group or an audience that did not receive the campaign. Without comparison, a rise in searches for the topic may be the news cycle, not the campaign.
A campaign report is one page: objective, baseline, result, cost per result and what would be done differently. Reach and engagement go in an appendix.
Break the result down by creator and by format. In the campaigns tracked, the gap between the most and the least efficient creator, measured in cost per action, was sixfold within the same campaign.
Record what did not work with the same precision as what did. An organization that only reports success cannot justify a change of strategy in the next campaign.

resumo: The climate terms that appear most in briefs and news, with their exact meaning and the misuse that repeats most often in videos.

paragrafos: Climate change: a long-term shift in temperature and rainfall patterns, measured over decades. One hotter summer is weather; thirty hotter summers is climate. Do not use 'climate change' to describe an unusual day.

Greenhouse gases: gases that trap heat in the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is the most cited, but methane traps far more heat per tonne in the short term and comes mostly from landfills, livestock and gas leaks. When the subject is a city, landfills and traffic usually weigh more than industry.

Net zero emissions: when what is emitted is offset by what is removed from the atmosphere. It is not the same as emitting zero. A company or city with a 'neutrality' target can keep emitting and pay for removal elsewhere; it is worth asking how much is reduction and how much is offsetting.

Mitigation and adaptation: mitigating is cutting emissions so the problem grows less; adapting is preparing the city for the problem that already exists. Planting trees for shade is adaptation; replacing diesel buses with electric ones is mitigation. Content that confuses the two suggests one can replace the other.

Heat island: an urban area hotter than its surroundings because of asphalt, concrete and lack of vegetation. The difference reaches several degrees at the same hour between neighborhoods of the same city. It is the right term to explain why one neighborhood suffers more than another in a heat wave.

Extreme event: rain, drought, heat or cold outside the historical range for the place. A single event does not prove climate change; a rising frequency of events does. When covering a flood, the correct wording is that events of this kind are becoming more frequent, not that this flood was caused by climate.

Vulnerability: how much a group or place suffers from the same event. Two streets with the same rainfall end up differently depending on drainage, income and housing type. Climate content that does not mention vulnerability tends to treat as equal what is not.

Carbon offsetting: paying for emission removal or reduction done by someone else. It serves what cannot be reduced and does not replace reduction. If a sponsor asks to call offsetting 'zero carbon', the correct term is 'offset'.

Green, sustainable, eco: no fixed definition and no rule of use. When they show up in a brief, ask for the data behind them: how much it reduces, compared with what, measured by whom. Without an answer, the word does not go in the script.

Energy transition: replacing fossil sources with renewables. It is not an event but a process with deadlines and costs, and the useful question for the public is who pays and when. Content that presents the transition as an individual consumer choice gets the scale of the problem wrong.
